content: Head injuries are a common occurrence and can lead to a wide range of motor and cognitive impairments. One frequent complication following head trauma is the development of seizures. Antiepileptic drugs (AEDs), such as phenytoin, are often prescribed in clinical settings with the aim of preventing post-traumatic epilepsy. However, it remains unclear whether the immediate use of AEDs or neuroprotective drugs after a head injury can influence the process of epileptogenesis and improve outcomes. This review sought to evaluate the effectiveness of these pharmacological interventions and builds upon a previous Cochrane review. The objective of this review was to compare the efficacy of AEDs and neuroprotective agents against placebo, standard care, or other pharmacological treatments in preventing post-traumatic epilepsy in individuals with traumatic brain injuries of any severity. The researchers conducted a comprehensive search of multiple databases, including the Cochrane Epilepsy Group's specialized register, CENTRAL, MEDLINE, ClinicalTrials.gov, and the World Health Organization International Clinical Trials Registry Platform (ICTRP) in January 2015. Additional searches were performed in EMBASE, Biological Abstracts, and the National Research Register in September 2014, and SCOPUS in December 2013. Relevant journals were also hand-searched by the Cochrane Epilepsy Group. The review included randomized controlled trials (RCTs) that compared AEDs or neuroprotective agents with placebo, other pharmacological agents, or standard care. The outcomes assessed included the occurrence of seizures within one week of trauma (early seizures), seizures occurring more than one week after trauma (late seizures), mortality, and adverse events. Two independent reviewers assessed the quality of the studies and extracted data. Risk ratios (RR) and 95% confidence intervals (CI) were calculated for each outcome. Meta-analyses were conducted using random-effects models, and pre-defined subgroup and sensitivity analyses were performed. The review included 10 RCTs (reported in 12 articles) involving a total of 2,326 participants. The methodological quality of the studies varied. The interventions were categorized into three groups: AEDs versus placebo or standard care, neuroprotective agents versus placebo or standard care, and comparisons between different AEDs. Treatment with AEDs, specifically phenytoin or carbamazepine, was associated with a reduced risk of early seizures compared to placebo or standard care (RR 0.42, 95% CI 0.23 to 0.73; very low-quality evidence). However, there was no evidence of a difference in the risk of late seizures between AEDs and placebo or standard care (RR 0.91, 95% CI 0.57 to 1.46; very low-quality evidence). Similarly, there was no significant difference in all-cause mortality between AEDs and placebo or standard care (RR 1.08, 95% CI 0.79 to 1.46; very low-quality evidence). Only one study evaluated a neuroprotective agent, magnesium sulfate, compared to placebo. The risk ratios for late seizures and all-cause mortality were 1.07 (95% CI 0.53 to 2.17) and 1.20 (95% CI 0.80 to 1.81), respectively. The risk ratio for early seizures could not be estimated. Two studies compared different AEDs, specifically levetiracetam and valproate, with phenytoin as the main comparator. The risk ratio for all-cause mortality was 0.53 (95% CI 0.30 to 0.94). There was no evidence of a treatment benefit of phenytoin over other AEDs for early seizures (RR 0.66, 95% CI 0.20 to 2.12) or late seizures (RR 0.77, 95% CI 0.46 to 1.30). Adverse events were reported in only two studies. The risk ratio for any adverse event with AEDs compared to placebo was 1.65 (95% CI 0.73 to 3.66; low-quality evidence). There were insufficient data on adverse events for other treatment comparisons. In conclusion, this review found low-quality evidence suggesting that early treatment with AEDs, compared to placebo or standard care, reduces the risk of early post-traumatic seizures. However, there was no evidence to support a reduction in the risk of late seizures or mortality. Additionally, there was insufficient evidence to draw conclusions about the effectiveness or safety of neuroprotective agents compared to placebo or the comparative efficacy of phenytoin versus other AEDs.
